  detection further.

  By the late 1990s it was clear that AIMD's halving behavior made
  classic TCP unable to fill high bandwidth-delay product paths: a flow
  at 10 Gbps over 100ms drops to ~4 Mbps after one loss, and would need
  tens of thousands of consecutive loss-free RTTs to climb back. That
  spawned a decade of high-speed proposals — HighSpeed TCP, BIC, and
  finally CUBIC, which replaced the linear increase with a cubic
  function of time since the last congestion event, probing aggressively
   right after a loss and cautiously as it approaches the previous
  maximum. CUBIC became the default on Linux in 2006 and remains the
  standard Linux stack, and it also underlies most non-Apple platforms'
  transports today.

  A parallel line of work questioned the loss-as-congestion premise
  itself, especially once wireless links and shallow-buffer datacenters
  entered the picture. In those environments loss often means bit errors
   or buffer pressure, not a saturated bottleneck. TCP Vegas, Westwood,
  and Compound TCP tried delay- or hybrid-based signals. The most
  influential result was BBR (Google, 2016), which models the path's
  bottleneck bandwidth and minimum RTT directly and paces traffic to sit
   at the BDP without filling buffers. BBR dramatically improves
  throughput and latency on lossy links (it initially caused fairness
  and bufferbloat controversies that BBRv2 and v3 address), and it now
  carries a large fraction of Google and Netflix traffic.

  The newest chapter is the kernel-to-userspace boundary: QUIC
  reimplements congestion control in userspace, letting applications
  like BBR or CUBIC with new loss detection ship independently of OS
  kernels, and IEEE 802.11's aggregation and 5G's buffer behavior keep
  producing tailored variants like BBRv2, Copa, and Swift.

  DONE
